claims.text: Separately modeling phonon and electronic transport will improve thermal-conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr relative to conventional Debye-based methods.
The intended material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr with minimized defects and controlled impurity levels.
Specimens containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen can fall within the approach's intended applicability.
DFT-derived phonon dispersions incorporating anharmonicity and disorder can be used to calculate lattice thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Independently calculated electronic band structures can be used to calculate the electronic thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
The model can apply impurity corrections appropriate to oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are nearly comparable.
The approach is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr at temperatures extending to approximately 1200 K.
Atomic-scale disorder and force-constant variations mediate phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electronic transport in HfNbTaTiZr is governed by its band-structure properties.
Explicitly separating phonon and electron contributions avoids oversimplifications associated with unified Debye-temperature scaling.
Accounting for temperature-dependent anharmonicity and disorder while treating the two transport channels independently reduces systematic prediction error.
The summed lattice and electronic predictions will match measured total conductivity values of 10–17 W/(K·m).
The approach will improve prediction error by roughly 10–20% relative to conventional methods.
The model will predict nearly equal lattice and electronic conductivity contributions below 200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr will shift toward lattice-dominated heat conduction at higher temperatures.
Earlier analytical and DFT-based approaches rely on single-parameter approximations such as Debye temperature and do not distinguish lattice and electronic contributions.
The approach is primarily reliable between approximately 50 and 1200 K for bulk concentrated alloys with limited defects and controlled impurities.
Significant defects or uncontrolled impurities will reduce the approach's reliability.
Time-domain thermoreflectance and electrical measurements combined with the Wiedemann–Franz relation can provide independent lattice and electronic conductivity values for the proposed validation.
